questiontext.text: How does a 4-ary heap differ from a binary heap?

answer.text: Each internal node has up to 4 children instead of 2

feedback.text: Correct — a d-ary heap generalizes the branching factor to d = 4.

answer.text: It stores 4 keys in every node

feedback.text: No — nodes still hold one key; only the fan-out changes.

answer.text: It drops the heap-order property

feedback.text: No — the heap property is unchanged.

answer.text: It must be stored with pointers, not an array

feedback.text: No — it still maps cleanly onto an array.

generalfeedback.text: A d-ary heap is a binary-heap generalization where each node has up to d children; a 4-ary heap uses d = 4.

questiontext.text: Compared with a binary heap on the same n elements, a 4-ary heap is:

answer.text: Shallower, with height about log_4 n

feedback.text: Correct — larger fan-out means fewer levels, height Θ(log_d n).

answer.text: Taller, with height about 4 log n

feedback.text: No — more children per node makes the tree shorter, not taller.

answer.text: The same height, log_2 n

feedback.text: No — the base of the logarithm changes to d.

answer.text: Always exactly 4 levels

feedback.text: No — height still grows with n, just more slowly.

generalfeedback.text: Height is Θ(log_d n); with d = 4 the tree is shallower than a binary heap.

questiontext.text: What is the extract-min cost of a d-ary heap, and why?

answer.text: O(d · log_d n), because sift-down compares all d children at each level

feedback.text: Correct — fewer levels but d comparisons per level to find the smallest child.

answer.text: O(log_d n), the same as insert

feedback.text: No — sift-down must scan all d children each level, adding a factor of d.

answer.text: O(1), because the root is the minimum

feedback.text: Finding the min is O(1), but removing and restoring is not.

answer.text: O(n), it must rescan the whole array

feedback.text: No — only one root-to-leaf path is traversed.

generalfeedback.text: Sift-down visits log_d n levels and compares d children at each, so extract-min is O(d log_d n) — larger d makes it costlier.

questiontext.text: For which workload is increasing d (e.g. a 4-ary heap) most beneficial?

answer.text: Decrease-key-heavy workloads such as Dijkstra's algorithm

feedback.text: Correct — cheaper O(log_d n) inserts/decrease-keys dominate the extra extract cost.

answer.text: Workloads that are almost all extract-min

feedback.text: No — extract-min gets more expensive as d grows.

answer.text: Workloads needing a stable sort

feedback.text: No — heaps are not about stability.

answer.text: Workloads with no priority operations at all

feedback.text: No — then you would not use a heap.

generalfeedback.text: Larger d cheapens insert/decrease-key (O(log_d n)) while making extract-min pricier, so it wins when decrease-key dominates, as in Dijkstra.

questiontext.text: A shallower 4-ary heap tends to be more cache-friendly than a binary heap.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — fewer levels and clustered children improve locality of reference.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Fewer levels and grouped children generally improve cache behavior.

questiontext.text: Insert (sift-up) is asymptotically cheaper in a 4-ary heap than in a binary heap because the tree is shallower.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — sift-up only compares against one parent per level, over O(log_d n) levels.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Sift-up compares only with the single parent each level, so fewer levels means less work.

questiontext.text: In a "d-ary heap", the letter ______ denotes the number of children each node may have.

answer.text: d

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: d*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a 4-ary heap are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Insert / decrease-key cost O(log_4 n)

feedback.text: Yes — sift-up over fewer levels.

answer.text: Extract-min costs O(4 · log_4 n) due to comparing 4 children per level

feedback.text: Yes — that d factor is the price of a larger fan-out.

answer.text: It cannot be stored in a flat array

feedback.text: No — index arithmetic generalizes: children of i are di-(d-2)..di+1 style formulas.

answer.text: Choosing d larger always speeds up every operation

feedback.text: No — larger d trades cheaper insert for costlier extract-min.

generalfeedback.text: A 4-ary heap makes insert/decrease-key cheaper (O(log_d n)) but extract-min costlier (O(d log_d n)); it still lives in an array, and tuning d is a trade-off, not a free win.
